class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Karolis Kaupinas, 38, a journalist turned filmmaker and playwright, sits in the lobby of the Lithuanian National Drama Theatre in Vilnius on April 14.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kaupinas has been busy with projects, including his new play, "Lithuanian Death Notices: The Story of a Performance," inspired by a Facebook page he'd seen of a Chicago funeral home.</p><p>But in September, alarm bells from his childhood went off.</p><p>The populist right-wing party Nemunas Dawn, which had been invited into a governing coalition by the center-left Social Democrats, tried to take over the culture ministry. Then there was a legislative attempt to curtail Lithuanian Radio and Television's editorial independence.</p><p>Kaupinas has helped lead protests for freedom of expression that have expanded across the country. Nemunas Dawn was kicked out of the government in June.</p><p>"I have two small kids now, and they're going to live here after me. And if I want them to have a happy life ... I need to leave it to them as good as I found it," Kaupinas says.</p><p>As for Americans, he hopes they reflect on how fragile freedom can be.</p><p>"Two hundred fifty years of democracy — I’ll make it a bit blunt — makes you lazy," he says. "Americans have been sent to wars, but they haven't seen something like that on their own land for quite some time. I think it's a natural cycle of a society to forget things that shouldn't be taken for granted. That's our danger as well. That's why we are trying to remember that freedom of speech, democracy — that might disappear. It's always easy to destroy things but very hard to create them, to rebuild them."</p><h3>Suburban hotline</h3><p>Watching the recent protests from Chicago's suburbs are George and Viligailė Lendraitis of Palos Heights and Rimas and Audronė Gulbinas of Winfield. The longtime friends helped play a role in bolstering Lithuania's independence 36 years ago.</p><p>Like many Lithuanian Americans in the Chicago area, their family members fled the country and spent decades praying for its independence.</p><p>The language classes, dance troupes and summer camps they joined kept diaspora Lithuanians connected to the culture. That's still the case: Several thousand people attended the Lithuanian Folk Dance Festival of North America in July at the McCormick Center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div like Lithuania's nascent independence movement might be crushed, the friends created the Lithuanian Hotline to push reports from Lithuania to U.S. government officials, the media and democracy supporters.</p><p>They established a command room at the Lithuanian World Center in Lemont, a 125,000-square-foot facility that hosts more than 50 Lithuanian organizations, including folk dancing groups, a Lithuanian language Montessori preschool and the Lituanica basketball club that helped produce Bulls star Matas Buzelis.</p><p>Illinois Bell hooked up the number they'll never forget: 708-257-6777.</p><p>"We didn’t want any false information going out," George Lendraitis, 77, says. "We were worried. We all have relatives there."</p><p>The hotline transitioned to Lithuanian Mercy Lift, a massive volunteer effort to ship nearly $127 million worth of medicine, medical equipment and other humanitarian supplies to support Lithuania over the next 20 years.</p><p>At a 2010 farewell event in Vilnius' Old Town, doctors, nurses and former President Valdas Adamkus — whose wife volunteered on the hotline when the couple lived in the Chicago suburbs — came out to thank the group.</p><p>"We were happy but exhausted after 20 years," George Lendraitis says. "It was a big part of our life."</p><p>Former Lithuanian President Dalia Grybauskaitė, visiting Chicago for the folk dance festival, called that Chicago support "very important" because it came from a Lithuanian community that also was a bridge to the West. </p><p>"For us, it was a dream about freedom, and this example of the U.S. was helping us to be strong," she says.</p><div class="Enhancement" "They can live in freedom. They can pursue their own goals. They can do what they want without some foreign government or some oppressor saying, 'No, you can't' — stopping people wherever they want to go. So that [American] example of freedom and of democracy flourishing here in Lithuania is really critical."</p><p>Tomas Morkus finished high school this year in Lithuania's second largest city, Kaunas. He spent the 2023-24 school year studying at St. Ignatius College Prep in Chicago on a full scholarship. He'll attend Brown University in the fall.</p><p>Having grown up hearing stories of relatives exiled to Siberia, Morkus says he recognizes that economic prosperity, democracy and defense are intertwined — and that they're worth protecting.</p><p>In high school, he volunteered on numerous projects, including an EU initiative to teach younger kids about the importance of democracy.</p><p>"There are plenty of examples from history where authoritarianism wins against weak democratic institutions or a weak civil society, and then horrible things follow, whether it's Soviet Russia, Hitler's Germany or anywhere else," he says.</p><p>Lithuanians, "still remember the days when they couldn't stand up for themselves and they were shut down for what they say or what they do or what they express," he says. "So I think definitely, the fight is there. The fight is actively going on. I’m proud to be a part of it."</p><p><i>Contributing: Ashlee Rezin</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-fullBleed> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a He spent the 2023-24 school year studying at St. Ignatius College Prep in Chicago and plans to attend Brown University in the fall.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>When Soviet soldiers stormed a TV station</h4><br>VILNIUS, Lithuania — On Jan. 13, 1991, Soviet troops stormed the building of Lithuania’s public broadcaster and pulled the plug during a live newscast.<br><br>A few minutes earlier, soldiers had begun shooting and driving tanks toward civilians who had gathered to defend the iconic 1,071-foot Vilnius TV Tower in another part of the capital. Fourteen people were killed and hundreds injured.<br><br>Archival video captured the moment, around 2 a.m., when Lithuanian Radio and Television anchor Eglė Bučelytė told viewers another group of soldiers had just breached their offices. <br><br>Soldiers streamed through the hallways.<br><br>“Dear people, this is the very last piece of information: The Lithuanian radio has stopped broadcasting, but television, as you can see, still is,” Bučelytė says.<br><br>But just as quickly, she’s gone; the broadcast shuts off.<br><br>Guoda Litvaitienė was a radio producer at LRT, assigned to work on programs for Lithuanians living abroad.<br><br>Litvaitienė, now 63 and editor-in-chief of LRT Radio, remembers the tense atmosphere that began two days earlier, when Soviet troops seized the National Defense Department building and the Press House, home to most of Lithuania’s newspapers and publishers.<br><br>Litvaitienė’s editor sent her and many other employees home, so she was glued to the same broadcast as everyone else in the country.<br><br>“It was horrible, and nobody knew what would be the ending — will they shoot or what? It was terrible,” she says.<br><br>The soldiers occupied the LRT building for more than seven months, beaming out Soviet propaganda.<br><br>But LRT’s journalists continued working from other locations. Within days, a makeshift TV studio and transmitter were set up at the barricaded parliament building in Vilnius, where legislators inside and citizens outside had managed to repel Soviet soldiers.<br><br>Litvaitienė’s public radio colleagues borrowed studios in Vilnius, offered by a library for blind people, and were able to continue broadcasting.<br><br>“Somehow [the public] knew where we were stationed, and they brought us cakes, some meals, flowers, money,” she says.<br><br>After the troops left, it took months to clean up their mess. Litvaitienė says employees found excrement inside destroyed audio equipment and archival tapes that were wrecked and lying on the floor.<br><br>The equipment was replaced, but the bullet holes in the building were left as a reminder for future generations.<br><br>A new battle over the future of Lithuania’s public broadcaster started late last year, after a far-right populist party installed one of their own at the Ministry of Culture. Parliament members tried to push through legislation that would freeze funding for public broadcasting, making it easier to fire LRT’s director general and compromise the broadcaster’s editorial independence.<br><br>Tens of thousands of people protested, and more than 145,000 people signed a petition in support of LRT’s independence.<br><br>The culture minister resigned after one week and was replaced, and some of the most controversial legislative proposals were withdrawn. class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f00000" name="module-f00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>A community still thriving</h4><br>VILNIUS, Lithuania — If there’s one idea Viljamas Žitkauskas would like Americans to know, it’s that the deep roots of the Litvaks — Lithuania’s Jewish community — didn’t disappear in World War II.<br><br>Rather, Jewish culture and creativity lives on in those who stayed after the Holocaust and in those who’ve chosen to return, Žitkauskas tells tourists on his Jewish history tours.<br><br>Lithuania had a thriving population of Litvaks, whose members included Rabbi Elijah ben Solomon Zalman, the famous 18th-century Talmudic scholar and mystic; artist Marc Chagall, born in Belarus to a family with Litvak roots; and the forebears of musicians Bob Dylan and Leonard Cohen.<br><br>Up to 95% of Lithuania’s Jews, about 195,000 people, were murdered by Nazis and their local collaborators when Germany occupied Lithuania from 1941 to 1944. Many historians view the killings as the beginning of the Nazis’ “Final Solution,” the genocide of European Jews during World War II.<br><br>Žitkauskas, who helped found the Vilnius Reform congregation Bnei Maskilim, says many tourists come to Lithuania to hear about the Holocaust but end up learning that Litvak history didn’t end there.<br><br>“For many people, they are coming to see the graveyard, and they’re realizing that it’s not really that. It’s a Jewish community, and there are people living here today, and it’s a big surprise for them,” he says.<br><br>Jewish people arrived in the 1300s, when it was the power center of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania — a sprawling, multiethnic empire that stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea and included Lithuania, Belarus, most of Ukraine and parts of Latvia, Poland, Moldova and Russia.<br><br>Signs of a Jewish presence are everywhere. Žitkauskas likes to point out the famous Vilnius Cathedral, adorned with figures of Moses, Abraham and Noah, Jewish figures from the Old Testament. Vilnius was also once called “the Jerusalem of the North.”<br><br>His family, with roots dating to the 1700s, escaped to Russia during the Holocaust but returned to Lithuania after the German army was driven out by the Soviets in 1944.<br><br>Žitkauskas was 10 years old when Lithuania declared its independence from the Soviet Union.<br><br>“I still remember the Russian tanks,” he says. “I’m still from the generation that really appreciates freedom.”<br><br>Žitkauskas offers tours for groups or individuals. His clients often hail from Israel, U.S., South Africa, Australia and Canada — places where Litvaks built new lives.<br><br>He tailors tours to visitors’ needs. If they’ve got old letters or diaries from ancestors who lived in the Baltic countries or Poland, he can take them to the places where their family members lived.<br><br>Some tourists want to dig into the history of famous Orthodox rabbis. Others want a more secular experience, like learning about Jewish art or comparing Lithuanian potato pancakes to the ones their Ashkenazi grandmother used to make.<br><br>“It’s very dependent on the needs and thoughts of customers — what they’re searching for,” he says.<br><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pulitzer Center</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div>Chicago Sun-Times investigative reporter Stephanie Zimmermann and photo editor Ashlee Rezin traveled to Lithuania for two weeks in April as the Pulitzer Center’s 2026 Richard C. Longworth Media fellows. Their aim was to shed light on a region with strong Chicago ties and an increasingly important role on the world stage.<br><br>A member of the European Union and NATO since 2004, Lithuania is a paradox. Its economic growth is in Europe’s top 25%, and it has six tech unicorns, startups valued at more than $1 billion. Yet the country of 2.8 million people is located at one of Europe’s most vulnerable spots for military defense.<br><br>Zimmermann interviewed more than 50 people for the six-story series, from a former president and a current foreign minister to ordinary Lithuanians living at a time of both promise and peril.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Why I traveled 4,700 miles from Chicago to Lithuania
entries.summary: <p>Why Lithuania?</p><p>That's the first thing my editor asked when I proposed applying for a Pulitzer Center grant for journalists to report international stories. The center's <a class="Link" href="https://pulitzercenter.org/blog/pulitzer-center-awards-2026-longworth-fellowships-2-chicago-journalists" target="_blank" >Richard C. Longworth Media Fellowships</a> help journalists write about global issues impacting Chicago and Midwestern readers.</p><p>Chicago has huge ties to the tiny nation northeast of Poland and across the Baltic Sea from Sweden. About 60,000 Lithuanian Americans live in the Chicago area.</p><p>Upton Sinclair's famous socialist novel "The Jungle" made me forever question eating sausage. Its protagonist, the exploited immigrant Jurgis Rudkus, who chased the American dream in Chicago, was Lithuanian.</p><p>Chicago has other famous Lithuanians: Valdas Adamkus, who became president of Lithuania twice; U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and Matas Buzelis, the Bulls star who played for Lituanica Athletic Club in Lemont as a kid.</p><p>Lithuania is relevant for other reasons, too.</p><p>Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, many in the U.S. have worried about what would happen if Russian President Vladimir Putin tried attacking a European NATO country. Lithuania, a NATO member since 2004, is a prime target; it's sandwiched between Russia's Kaliningrad and Putin's ally Belarus.</p><p>Meanwhile, Lithuanians are known for sticking their necks out for democracy. Chicagoans helped with that when the country pushed for independence, which we should remember as America celebrates its 250th anniversary.</p><p>But there was another reason I wanted to go.</p><p>My late mother was born in Lithuania. She fled as a child when the Soviet reoccupation began in 1944.</p><p>My cellphone's screensaver is a photo of my mom as a baby, sitting on an unused beehive box (honey is big in Lithuania) with her smiling dad standing next to her.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-330000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Stephanie Zimmermann</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>So, with the blessing of the Chicago Sun-Times, I packed my bags and set off in April with Sun-Times photojournalist and editor Ashlee Rezin.</p><p>This was my third trip to Lithuania. I have cousins there, and I've been learning the language, though almost one-third of Lithuanians speak English.</p><p>I was amazed by the generosity of Lithuanians I met. They spent hours talking to me about democracy, defense, history, economics, Adamkus' legacy and how their small country produces so many big basketball stars.</p><p>Maybe their generosity was because American media too often ignores this nation of just 2.8 million people.</p><p>We met Adamkus, who is turning 100 in November, at his elegant home in the woods on the edge of the capital, Vilnius. The former president had been the regional U.S. Environmental Protection Agency administrator in Chicago. He talked about his favorite Chicago newspapers (I gave him a Sun-Times tote bag) and wanted to know how the Deep Tunnel was faring.</p><p>I also interviewed the foreign minister, economics minister, several parliamentarians, including a signer of the 1990 independence declaration, academics, local officials, business leaders, lawyers, journalists and artists.</p><p>I spoke with ordinary people such as a driving instructor, a civics teacher, flea market sellers and high school and college students. More than 50 people shared their perspectives.</p><p>I learned Lithuanians are in a "dangerous neighborhood," meaning where they sit geographically.</p><p>Even though they prepare for the worst, they're proud to live in a country experiencing economic growth, where young people were deemed the "world’s happiest."</p><p>In addition to Vilnius, our reporting took us to Kaunas, the second largest city and the heart of Lithuanian basketball; Klaipėda on the Baltic Sea; the town of Kybartai, bordering Kaliningrad; a Sunday flea market in Kalvarija, a short drive from the Suwalki Gap; Trakai, home of Lithuania's most picturesque castle; and the town of Kazlų Rūda, deep in the pine forests.</p><p>One Sunday morning, we were driving on the back roads of southwest Lithuania with our translator, Karolis Vyšniauskas.</p><p>Vyšniauskas was planning to turn left, heading for Kalvarija, when the road got rough, so we went straight.</p><p>About 100 yards later, I yelled, "Stop!"</p><p>A road sign read "Pajevonys," a name that seemed vaguely familiar. I flipped through my grandparents' memoirs, which I'd packed with my reporting notes.</p><p>My hunch was right. They lived in Pajevonys when my mom was a baby. My grandparents were teachers, and they frequently moved to different towns for jobs.</p><p>Within a few years, they would flee Lithuania. Theirs is a story shared by many in the diaspora: They were "displaced persons" in camps in Germany at the end of World War II. My mom spent her childhood in Germany, then won a college scholarship to study in America and later became a naturalized American citizen.</p><p>Vyšniauskas pulled over, and I hopped out of the car to touch the sign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-340000" name="image-340000"></a> entries.title: Food brings this family together, but one particular recipe reminds them of home
entries.summary: <p>Food has been at the center of Teddy and Alexis Vejar’s lives since they were kids.</p><p>They remember walking around their neighborhood in Morelia, Michoacán, where people would open up their driveways or garages and serve dinner out of their homes.</p><p>When they moved to Chicago in the 1990s, their dad — who they call “the original Mexican foodie” — still searched far and wide for the best food he could find.</p><p>“We would literally drive from Chicago all the way to Oaxaca, and my dad would say, ‘We’re going to try cabrito (suckling goat),’” Alexis Vejar said. “We would take detours for specific dishes. We would go all the way to Veracruz just to try the pescado a la Veracruzana.”</p><p>Today, the brothers own Jarabe. The restaurant opened in 2015 and prides itself on authentic Mexican cuisine. You won’t find any “fancy tacos” at the Little Italy spot.</p><p>“We could do fancy tacos,” Alexis Vejar said. “But what’s ridiculously good? What my grandma used to do — harvesting the corn, milking the cow, making the cheese, making sour cream. That's more hard work than a Michelin-star restaurant is prepared to do.”</p><p>The brothers have spent 15 years building a menu they can be proud of, and every recipe traces back to what they learned from their parents and grandparents.</p><p>When they began developing their recipes, they focused on making things from scratch, like tortillas and marinades, even when it was more difficult.</p><p>Of all the dishes they grew up eating, one remains their favorite all these years later: cochinita pibil. They serve it at their restaurant.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>Teddy and Alexis have fond memories living in Chicago’s Ukrainian Village, when their dad began making homemade cochinita pibil for them and their extended family. Even today, the family gets together to eat the dish.</p><p>Cochinita pibil is a Yucatán-style pulled pork dish. The pork is marinated in achiote paste and served with tortillas and pickled red onions. It’s considered one of Yucatán’s traditional dishes, and it’s a favorite celebration meal for the Vejar family.</p><p>The dish reminds them of when their dad would cook it for them when they were kids.</p><p>“My dad's really into analyzing dishes and seeing how you can improve them, so that was part of the fun,” Alexis Vejar said. “It's something that Teddy and I ate a lot in Morelia because there was one puestito that sold cochinita pibil. We just rolled up to the tiny place that sold these tiny little tacos with the little red onions on top. We were obsessed with them. It just reminded us so much of home.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/07/22/cochinita-pibil-recipe" >Bring this cochinita pibil recipe to your next family dinner</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Looking back to their time in Mexico, Alexis and Teddy reflected on how simple the recipes seemed in theory, though they now realize the immense time and process everything entailed. Corn was grown and harvested, then went through the nixtamalization process — a tradition they maintain at their restaurant today to craft their own homemade tortillas.</p><p>“Every time we visited my grandma, she was waking up and making homemade bread with natural yeast that she was cultivating in a wood-burning oven,” Alexis Vejar said. “If we had sour cream or cheese, she milked the cow to make it. If we had meat, it was meat that they raised, that they butchered, that they cured. The menus were all limited by what was available on the farm.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/OazrsIWZC3Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Tastes from Home: Tortillas, togetherness and time well spent."></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Even after years in business, Alexis and Teddy say they're still learning and growing.</p><p>Running a restaurant is nonstop, but they remain committed to honoring the family traditions that started long before Jarabe opened.</p><p>“We haven't slowed down. We're just getting started,” Alexis Vejar said. “It feels like we're still in the beginning.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure
